Reading guide

Preface: How to read this book

Chapter outline
  • A task to follow across the book
  • Three reading routes
  • Diagrams, examples, and evidence
  • Terms and chapter ownership
  • Method and reference project

This book examines the public OpenAI Codex repository at commit e4568a3538c9cab6627d64ff8cdfc7d98b79b7db, dated October 19, 2026. Research records are dated October 20, 2026. Source links point to that snapshot, keeping paths, symbols, defaults, and experimental conditions within one version. Recheck them when reading newer code.

The engineering question is how open-ended model actions enter a runtime with identity, lifecycles, cancellation, recovery, and authorization boundaries. The book assumes experience reading types, asynchronous control flow, and tests. It does not require prior knowledge of the Rust workspace or attempt to explain every file line by line.

A task to follow across the book

The recurring scenario asks Codex to fix a pagination function's empty-input behavior in a repository. Work might include locating code, reading conventions, editing files, and checking results. The user may add instructions, refuse an action, or stop the turn. Returning to the same scenario helps connect mechanisms across chapters.

The scenario is hypothetical. Model replies, commands, and patch sequences do not report a real model run or changes to a case-study repository. Teaching pseudocode is labelled as such and retains relevant boundary conditions; it is not presented as a callable Codex API.

Three reading routes

For an overview, read Chapter 1 through Chapter 3 for entry points, configuration, and state lifetimes. Continue from Chapter 4 through Chapter 6 to follow a model request and tool feedback. Choose the areas relevant to your work afterward, then use Chapter 19 and Chapter 20 to examine verification and design tradeoffs.

If you are building a runtime, start with the agent loop and tool contracts. Continue through concurrency, execution, and approval and sandboxing, then add persistence and engineering verification. Return to threads and turns when ownership or terminology is unclear. A copied handler still needs the surrounding lifecycle.

For a specific gap in an existing system, use context and memory for growing input; skills and plugins, MCP, and child agents for capabilities; or TUI, App Server, and SDKs for user and program interfaces. Each chapter ends with five design lessons that include applicable problems and costs.

Diagrams, examples, and evidence

Chapters explain normal behavior along with failures, cancellation, and boundary cases. Mermaid diagrams show control, state, or data relationships. A teaching state diagram can summarize several fields without implying a same-named source enum. Interactive panels are simplified explanations, not real schedulers or security decision engines.

Nearby source links support particular claims. Each chapter's "Reading the source" section provides further entry points. A cited range still needs to be read with its branch, callers, configuration conditions, and tests. The book favors implementations that own a behavior; a directory layout alone is not evidence of a call path.

A test assertion demonstrates intended coverage. Executing the test supplies a result for that environment. This Codex research is based on read-only source analysis: we did not run Codex tests or benchmarks and have no real-model repair success-rate data. Checks of the book's links, diagrams, HTML, and EPUB belong to its delivery records and are separate from tests of Codex itself.

Feature, platform, provider, and experimental conditions are part of the conclusions they qualify. Public client code shows request preparation, tool execution, and event recovery. It does not reveal all remote-model internals or server implementation. Interpretations of design motives are identified as interpretations or inferences. An optimization without measurement is explained as a mechanism, with no invented effect size.

Terms and chapter ownership

A thread is a conversation unit, distinct from an operating-system thread. A turn can contain several model steps. A step corresponds to a model sampling request and the settings and capabilities it captures. Rollout denotes recorded thread history; approval and sandbox denote separate authorization and isolation mechanisms. The glossary and source map collects definitions and links to the chapters that explain them fully.

Each mechanism has a main chapter. Other chapters locate it within their own request path and link to that explanation. This supports both sequential reading and investigation of a particular problem without maintaining several drifting definitions.

Method and reference project

Claude Code from Source informed the research and organization: investigate before planning and writing, organize chapters around questions, and combine diagrams, teaching pseudocode, transferable lessons, and source-reading guides. The reference version is fixed at a6d5e452a8e0dd925c22c407c84611b1994562eb.

Codex mechanism claims come from this book's pinned source snapshot. The original Chinese manuscript, diagrams, and reader were independently created for Codex; the reference project's prose, code, cover, and website components were not copied as material.

Chapter 01 · Runtime foundations

Chapter 1: Following a request through Codex

Chapter outline
  • Where the program begins
  • Read crates by responsibility
  • Four lifetimes within one task
  • Follow the repair request
  • Three message paths
  • Failure exposes ownership
  • Tests, feature conditions, and compatibility
  • Reading the source
  • Design lessons
  • Interactive panel: Responsibilities along a request path

Suppose you give Codex a repository and ask: "Fix the pagination function's empty-input edge case. Explain the cause first, then change the code and check the result." The request names no file, command, or patch. Completing it may require finding an entry point, reading repository conventions, running commands, and editing files. Missing dependencies or insufficient permissions may interrupt the work. You might add another instruction halfway through: "Keep the public interface unchanged." The program has to leave room for those choices while keeping execution in a defined order.

The model proposes what to do next. The runtime turns those proposals into work whose progress can be followed. It must decide which thread owns a request, whether new input starts a turn or joins one already running, and whether the tools advertised to the model match the tools available for execution. It also has to know who owns a background process or log writer after an interruption.

The pagination repair is a teaching scenario used throughout this book. Its commands, model replies, and patches do not describe a task we have executed. All source claims refer to commit e4568a3, dated October 19, 2026. The public code supports claims about that snapshot; it does not expose backend internals or establish product behavior outside it.

Where the program begins

At a terminal, codex looks like one program. Its source entry point is a dispatcher. main delegates to arg0_dispatch_or_else, and an ordinary invocation proceeds to cli_main. With no subcommand, it launches the interactive interface. The exec branch takes the noninteractive path. Other subcommands have their own purposes. Before following any call stack, identify the branch in the CLI dispatcher.

This snapshot also differs from some older architectural descriptions: exec creates an InProcessAppServerClient. The interactive interface connects through an App Server client too, with an in-process service, a local daemon, or a remote service as its target. App Server is therefore a logical protocol boundary. Both interfaces cross that boundary, and an in-process deployment does not require a separate operating-system process. The exec startup and TUI backend types show both sides.

Explore the mechanism in your browser. This panel does not execute Codex. Scenarios and values are illustrative; the chapter and source give the full conditions.

The three service paths are alternative deployment locations; they need not all exist at once. The remote model also remains outside local core. Public client code shows how Codex constructs requests, interprets events, and constrains actions. It cannot explain why the server-side model chose a particular action. Keeping that evidence boundary in view prevents a client branch from becoming an unsupported promise about model capabilities.

Read crates by responsibility

The Rust workspace contains many crates. A crate is a compilation and dependency unit, so its name does not necessarily identify a product feature or an independent process. On a first reading, ask what each layer accepts, what state it owns, and what it passes onward.

cli selects the operating mode. tui and exec determine how input and output are used. app-server translates external requests into operations on core objects. core handles session lifecycles, turn scheduling, model steps, and tool feedback. protocol and app-server-protocol define the relevant internal messages and external interface types. Model transport continues into client and API code. Actions pass through tool routing, execution environments, policy, and sandboxes; history crosses a persistence boundary. Responsibilities can span directories, so this is a guide to ownership rather than a one-directory-per-feature rule.

A small constraint makes the separation concrete: the top of the core crate forbids library code from printing directly to standard output or standard error. User-visible information should go through the interface or tracing abstractions. That dependency rule keeps the event separate from its presentation. A terminal can render a tool result, while a programmatic consumer can inspect the same result without making execution code aware of terminal layout. The core output rule enforces this separation.

These layers add work for a debugger. A single user message crosses several types and adapters, and protocol request IDs, core submission IDs, and model response IDs must be distinguished. In return, each layer can define its own completion condition. The interface does not have to infer whether finishing a model stream also finishes the repair task.

Four lifetimes within one task

Four lifetimes help organize the core. A thread is an identifiable, discoverable conversation unit; it is distinct from an operating-system thread. ThreadManager creates threads and keeps their live instances in memory. Callers receive a CodexThread handle containing the session object, communication endpoints, startup metadata, and an optional rollout path. The definitions of ThreadManager and CodexThread establish management and access boundaries.

Session is the live runtime for a thread. It holds state, services, the input queue, and the active turn. A turn is an accepted work lifecycle, from processing input until normal completion or abort. One turn can make many model requests. A model step captures the environment, model settings, and capabilities for one sampling request. Locating the pagination bug, reading a file through a tool, and asking the model what to do with the result may all belong to the same turn.

The arrows express management and capture relationships, not exclusively direct struct ownership. StepContext, in particular, captures a settings version, environment, MCP binding, final tool router, and the AGENTS.md files seen by that request. This binds the tools visible to the model to the tools used to execute its calls at the request boundary. Some authorization still comes from the parent turn's grant store. A captured snapshot does not freeze every related object forever, as the StepContext fields make explicit.

Separating state by lifetime limits how far a change can spread. Thread preferences can affect future turns. The current turn keeps its identity and output constraints. An issued model request has a record of the tools and environment it used. The cost appears when settings change: the implementation must say which work is affected immediately. Updating one global variable cannot supply that contract. Chapter 3 follows this question in detail.

Follow the repair request

The interface or script first collects the repair request as structured user content. The external service interface packages the input, thread settings, and startup options into a TurnInputRequest, then calls start_or_steer_turn. Core decides whether it can accept the request and which turn should receive it before contacting the model. The App Server mapping is the handoff from an interface request to the agent lifecycle.

SessionIo gives communication a defined shape: a submission sender, an event receiver, a status observation endpoint, and a shared completion future. Startup creates a bounded submission queue and an unbounded event queue, then starts the background submission_loop. That loop dispatches queued operations by type. User input, interrupts, approval replies, settings updates, and shutdown have different handlers. The queue orders dispatch of core operations; model requests and tool work need not execute synchronously inside that loop. The endpoints and background loop are the starting point for understanding concurrency later.

The first receipt confirms a routing decision. The source contract for Started and Steered says they do not wait for user prompt hooks, in-memory context updates, rollout persistence, or model sampling. Once a client receives Started, it can report that the work was accepted. It cannot report that the input is safely on disk or that the model has already seen it. The receipt contract separates these confirmation points.

This teaching pseudocode retains those boundaries. It is not a callable API:

# Teaching pseudocode: from input to a turn
request = collect_user_content_and_settings()
decision = core_accept_and_route(request)
display_receipt(decision)
if decision is rejected: return
for each event:
    update_current_turn_display(event)
    if event terminates the turn: stop_waiting

Once the turn starts, the runtime shapes the current history into model input, captures the model step, and issues a streaming request. The model may return text or tool calls. Tool results enter the context and become input to the next request. Continuation depends on more than the presence of tool calls: the runtime also considers pending input, budgets, and stop hooks. In run_turn, needs_follow_up combines the model's request for further work with the existence of pending input. The continuation check explains why a finished model response can leave the turn running.

This is how the model participates in the loop. It proposes the next action; the runtime determines how to encode it, whether it may execute, how its result enters history, and when work may stop. Chapter 8 follows actual file changes. Chapter 9 covers approvals and sandboxes, whose enforcement requires runtime mechanisms beyond instructions in a prompt.

Three message paths

The end-to-end diagram carries several kinds of message. Operations from a consumer to the runtime include user input, approval replies, and interrupts. Requests and stream events between runtime and model include model input, tool declarations, output items, text deltas, call arguments, and usage. Events from runtime to consumer report turn starts, tool progress, warnings, errors, and termination. There are more subprotocols in the implementation, but distinguishing these three paths prevents many reading mistakes.

"Keep the function signature" travels on the first path. The model's "I'll find its callers first" may arrive as text deltas on the second. The third path and its adapters organize what the interface displays and how it reports current work. A model sentence that sounds final cannot replace a core turn-termination event. Conversely, the interface can show progress while text is still arriving.

The model stream types preserve these distinctions. ResponseEvent includes OutputTextDelta, OutputItemDone, and Completed. Text deltas support incremental display. A completed output item supplies structure that the runtime can process. Response completion carries usage and an optional end_turn. The ResponseEvent definition lets consumers handle presentation, execution, and control separately.

These boundaries suggest concrete debugging questions. If the terminal shows no text, did the model stream contain deltas, or did the interface fail to project deltas it received? If no patch appeared, was there a complete call item, did routing succeed, or did a permissions boundary block execution? If the response ended but the interface remains busy, is there pending input or follow-up tool work? Each question identifies an owner and an observable event.

Configuration and instructions also have different effects. AGENTS.md can tell the model to keep the public interface stable. Runtime configuration selects the model, environment, permissions, and other executable settings. Calling both "context" hides where an operation was refused. Even when project trust permits a project configuration layer to take effect, sensitive keys are still filtered. A project instruction cannot replace that filter. The project configuration restrictions lead into the next chapter.

Failure exposes ownership

While the model reads the pagination function, you add "Keep the function signature." This input need not create a second turn. StartOrSteer can add it to an active ordinary turn. Explicit steering can also require a target turn ID and return a typed rejection when that ID does not match. This prevents a delayed interface action from silently reaching the next piece of work.

An interrupt introduces another boundary. The runtime must cancel the active task and release work waiting for approval, user input, or a tool result. Stopping an animation would leave those resources active. The source also specifies an ordering: let the task observe cancellation before clearing pending input and waiters. Otherwise, the disappearance of an approval sender could first become a denial visible to the model. The cancellation order returns in the concurrency chapter.

Failure can occur before a thread finishes starting. Startup may already own a log writer while extension initialization is still blocked, and the caller may then drop the startup future. SessionStartupGuard retains cleanup responsibility. Depending on whether control has reached the session loop, it either requests normal shutdown or cleans up partially initialized persistence resources. Without that path, a later resume could encounter resources left occupied by the failed startup. The startup cleanup branch gives incomplete initialization its own lifecycle.

# Teaching pseudocode: each stage confirms its own fact
acceptance_receipt != input_persisted
model_response_complete != turn_complete
turn_interrupted != session_closed
if initialization is partial:
    clean_up_according_to_current_resource_ownership()
    retain_lifecycle_responsibility_until_cleanup_handoff_finishes()

After reading a successful path, look for cancellation, rejection, and shutdown. Inspect the payload of any event whose name sounds like success. In this snapshot, TurnComplete can carry a terminal error, while TurnAborted gives an explicit abort reason. A client that treats an enum name alone as task success discards facts already supplied by the runtime.

Tests, feature conditions, and compatibility

The following chapters expand this request path: how startup assembles trusted configuration and instructions, how a turn owns state, and how model I/O, tools, execution, and context fit together. Later chapters return to interfaces and verification. At each boundary, ask what it protects.

Tests can clarify those contracts even when they are only being read. A core concurrent-input test uses a blockable fake SSE service to arrange two simultaneous submissions. It expects one Started receipt and one Steered receipt sharing the same turn ID, then inspects the follow-up request body for both messages. This connects routing and timing to the actual model input. Here we examine the test design and assertions without running the test or treating it as a production concurrency benchmark.

Also distinguish code that exists from code that is enabled. A tool handler in the repository does not guarantee that the current model request declares that tool. A compiled feature branch need not be enabled in session configuration. Remote-connection code in the TUI does not imply that every terminal launch contacts a remote App Server. Platform, provider, and experimental conditions belong beside the claims they qualify.

Compatibility names require similar care. Core still exports the deprecated ConversationManager, NewConversation, and CodexConversation aliases, mapped to the newer Thread terminology. Searching them can help locate callers. They do not establish another parallel "Conversation runtime." A fixed commit lets us inspect one coherent set of code relationships instead of combining names from different periods.

As you read, keep a timeline of who acquired a resource, accepted work, sent a request, observed a result, and finally released responsibility. That timeline makes a large workspace easier to investigate: each transition has an owner and a contract to check.

Reading the source

  • cli/main.rs: main and subcommand dispatch. Identify the entry point in use.
  • tui/lib.rs: AppServerTarget and connection fallback. Check the conditions for in-process, local, and remote paths.
  • exec/lib.rs: in-process client startup. Follow the service boundary used by the noninteractive entry point.
  • codex_thread.rs: CodexThread. Separate the public handle from the internal runtime.
  • session/mod.rs: SessionIo. Inspect input, output, status, and completion endpoints.
  • protocol/turn_input.rs: TurnInputSubmission. Read each receipt's guarantees and rejection reasons.
  • session/turn.rs: continuation checks. Distinguish a model response from a complete turn.
  • turn_input_submission.rs: concurrent-input test. Follow the fake stream through to assertions on the request body.

Design lessons

  1. Name state by its lifetime. When preferences, active tasks, and individual requests share one object, consider separate thread, turn, and request snapshots. Updates then need explicit scope; a small one-shot script may not need every layer.
  2. Model acceptance and completion separately. An API that returns before work ends needs a routing receipt followed by a termination event. Clients must handle both, and acceptance must not be mistaken for proof of persistence.
  3. Let interfaces consume typed events. A shared runtime can serve a terminal and a programmatic API through adapters. This requires event compatibility and a strategy for slow consumers.
  4. Assign cleanup ownership during initialization. Startup that acquires writers, connections, and background tasks needs an owner for every partial state. The longer failure path prevents resources from being forgotten when startup never succeeds.
  5. Check lifecycle contracts with controlled timelines. Gates and fake events can force concurrent-input and interruption order, then expose the final request or stored result for assertions. That infrastructure needs maintenance; text snapshots alone cannot establish lifecycle behavior.

Chapter 02 · Runtime foundations

Chapter 2: Startup, configuration, and trust

Chapter outline
  • The process identifies its role
  • Keep provenance with configuration values
  • A project cannot establish its own trust
  • Login and trust can require reassembly
  • AGENTS.md follows the directory chain
  • Cache invalidation follows access boundaries
  • Read failures as assembly contracts
  • Reading the source
  • Design lessons
  • Interactive panel: Two loading rules for the same project trust

Before a request can reach the session runtime, Codex must know where it is working, which model to use, which environments it can access, and which repository instructions to show the model. In the pagination repair, a wrong working directory could select the wrong AGENTS.md. A different configuration source could change the model or permissions. Both decisions precede the first model request.

Startup interprets files, command-line arguments, administrator requirements, authentication state, and user choices as executable configuration. It also needs enough provenance to explain why a value took effect. Codex retains configuration layers, origins, versions, disabled reasons, and independent constraints. These explain a common troubleshooting problem: editing a configuration file does not necessarily change the running behavior.

For this teaching scenario, assume the working directory is packages/pager and the task is still to fix the empty-input case. The path illustrates discovery rules; it does not refer to a project created or executed for this book. Most of this chapter follows local configuration assembly. Remote workspaces, enterprise configuration, and platform-specific paths have additional conditions.

The process identifies its role

The CLI's main first enters arg0_dispatch_or_else. This layer inspects the executable name and special arguments. The same executable can be invoked as a Linux sandbox helper, a patch tool, or another execution helper. A matching identity selects that helper's entry point; an ordinary invocation creates a runtime and proceeds to the CLI. Linux, Unix, and Windows branches retain their platform conditions. The identity dispatcher explains why the executable path is itself part of the execution environment.

The ordinary path builds a Tokio runtime on an operating-system thread named codex-main, with a stack budget for top-level asynchronous work. This OS thread is distinct from the conversation threads discussed elsewhere in the book. Arg0DispatchPaths carries the executable and helper paths onward. A guard keeps the temporary alias directory alive until the entry-point future finishes, so later execution does not reference a path already removed. Runtime startup and path retention document these lifetimes.

Within cli_main, feature enable and disable arguments become configuration overrides passed to the selected subcommand. Converting startup flags early into a representation downstream code already understands avoids implementing feature precedence at every layer. Other inputs remain typed: the core builder also takes harness overrides and loader options. Command-line input is therefore broader than a collection of TOML strings.

Keep provenance with configuration values

ConfigBuilder::build_inner resolves Codex home, makes the explicit or fallback cwd absolute, loads the layer stack, and constructs Config. The cwd already affects project discovery here. It is not deferred until a tool reads the process working directory. The builder's assembly order makes the working directory an input to configuration interpretation.

ConfigLayerSource::precedence defines ordinary layer priority. The following order runs from lowest to highest. Whether a source exists depends on the platform, installation, and current options.

Priority Configuration source Conditions
Lowest Bundled defaults Installation bundles can supply them; embedded defaults also exist
Higher MDM and system configuration The MDM branch requires the relevant platform support
Higher Enterprise cloud configuration Requires a corresponding bundle source
Higher User configuration and selected user profile The profile layer has priority over base user settings
Higher Project configuration Subject to trust checks and sensitive-key filtering
Higher SessionFlags Current-session overrides from the CLI, UI, and similar callers
Highest Legacy managed file and legacy managed MDM Compatibility layers for older managed formats still have higher priority

In this snapshot, legacy managed layers can override SessionFlags, so command-line input does not universally win. Administrator requirements also have an independent channel. Requirements can constrain allowed selections and participate in provider definitions, beyond overwriting ordinary values. After effective_config merges enabled layers, it may apply required provider definitions. Final configuration construction continues to apply selection requirements and other constraints. Read the precedence definition with the effective configuration calculation.

Each ConfigLayerEntry retains its source, content version, and optional disabled_reason. Effective configuration and per-key origins use enabled layers. Disabled layers remain available to explain why a file was discovered but not used. The per-key origin map excludes the separate requirements channel, so it cannot explain every policy decision on its own. Provenance may not help the model write a patch, but it helps a person explain the system's behavior.

# Teaching pseudocode: carry values and provenance together
layers = read_applicable_configuration_sources()
for each project_layer:
    record_trust_decision_and_disabled_reason()
    remove_keys_the_project_may_not_supply()
effective = merge_enabled_layers_by_precedence(layers)
config = apply_typed_overrides_and_independent_requirements(effective)
return config, layer_provenance(layers)

Suppose the user layer selects one model and a trusted project layer selects another. Higher overrides and requirements still determine the final selection. If the project layer is disabled, its model value never participates in merging. Troubleshooting should trace discovery, layer enablement, key filtering, later overrides, and requirements in that order. Repeatedly editing one value may never reach the decision that controls it.

Merging also has field-specific semantics. The general TOML branch recursively merges tables and overwrites other values. Some features accept either a boolean or a table of parameters; their merge code preserves enabled semantics across those representations. Network-domain and shell-filter paths have normalization rules of their own. Precedence establishes which layer has authority, while each field's representation and merge rules establish the resulting value. The merge implementation collects these exceptions at explicit paths.

This matters when configuration evolves. If an old feature was a boolean and a newer version adds parameters, replacing the entire value could make a change to one parameter erase its enablement state. Field-specific rules reconcile those forms. They also make the configuration system a domain model with its own behavior. An editor or administration interface must follow those semantics; structural similarity to JSON is insufficient reason to merge values independently.

Selected values and permitted values are separate. With no explicit approval policy, one source branch chooses a default and checks it against requirements. If the default is disallowed, it records a warning and uses the requirements-provided default. That fallback does not establish that every invalid explicit value is silently repaired. The retired public setting approval_policy="untrusted", for example, is explicitly rejected. An internal compatibility enum does not make it a supported configuration recommendation. The default-and-requirements branch separates these contracts.

A project cannot establish its own trust

Discovery has a deliberate order. Applicable non-project sources determine project roots and trust before project layers load. Managed sources participate at their applicable precedence during this stage. Repository content therefore cannot first rewrite the root markers or trust basis and then use that arrangement to authorize itself. The discovery order explains more than a list of possible file locations would.

The loader collects ancestors from cwd toward the project root, reverses them, and checks .codex directories from root toward cwd. Trust lookup considers normalized keys for locations including the current directory, project root, and repository root. An explicit Trusted decision passes the relevant project-layer check. Both explicit Untrusted and an unknown decision produce disabled reasons, with different explanations. "No decision yet" and "explicitly refused" have distinct meanings.

Teaching assumptions: files exist, formats are valid, read access is available, and documents fit the budget. This compares two entry conditions. Unknown trust does not establish full authorization, and the panel does not make real permission decisions.

Project configuration requires Trusted, then still filters sensitive keys such as model_provider. Project AGENTS.md is skipped on explicit Untrusted; unknown trust does not satisfy that explicit skip condition. Document access also depends on discovery, permissions, and budget.

Trust condition for configuration layersSensitive-key filtering after trustExplicit Untrusted condition for project instructions

Explore the mechanism in your browser. This panel does not execute Codex. Scenarios and values are illustrative; the chapter and source give the full conditions.

A trusted source still passes through a second filter. The project denylist covers model providers, related base URLs, notify, profiles, otel, and other configuration. Source comments explain that a project file should not decide where user credentials are sent or select arbitrary local commands. Filtering also handles nested fields. Environment-variable rules associated with the credential broker have additional enablement conditions; they do not imply a universal ban on project environment variables. The sensitive-key entry point and sanitize_project_config define the actual restriction.

Trust answers whether a source may supply the relevant project capabilities. Key filtering answers which controls that source may exercise even after trust is granted. The allocation of authority suggests a separation between repository work conventions and credential routing. That is an inference from the enforced boundary, not a claim to know every design motive behind it.

Trust also affects parse failures. A trusted project layer with invalid TOML returns an error. An untrusted or undecided layer can remain as an empty disabled layer, so an inactive malformed file does not prevent startup. Unknown-field behavior has another condition: strict checking of CLI overrides runs when strict_config is true. Its error behavior must not be generalized to every default load. The parse branches and strict-mode condition support separate claims.

Login and trust can require reassembly

Startup can revisit configuration. The interactive interface may first obtain initial configuration and a service connection, then handle login, choose a target thread, and establish trust for its actual destination. Folder consent occurs after the picker has chosen that destination. This avoids obtaining consent for one directory and beginning work in another.

After local login, the TUI refreshes the cloud configuration bundle where applicable and rebuilds configuration, so enterprise policy available only after login can participate. A persisted directory-trust change also triggers reloading. Remote workspaces have their own services and authentication policy; changing a local file does not establish that the remote execution environment changed. A narrower branch handles provider changes: when a reload selects a different provider and the current service is Embedded, the code shuts down the old service and starts one from the new configuration. Post-login rebuilding and destination trust handling show this feedback into startup.

Authentication itself lives in service objects such as AuthManager. It holds cached state, storage mode, administrator restrictions, external authentication providers, and refresh synchronization. It can notify consumers when authentication or the owner revision changes. auth_cached() reads the cache only. auth() may resolve external authentication again or perform a protected refresh for credentials requiring proactive renewal. These contracts extend beyond reading an API-key string. See the authentication state and read methods.

Authentication ownership also affects connection reuse. When the model client starts a new turn session, it compares the auth owner generation. A changed owner clears the old WebSocket cache, protecting the relationship between account identity and connection routing. Token expiry alone would not describe this rule. Providers have different authentication paths; later chapters examine recovery. At startup, keep three facts separate: configuration was assembled, authentication exists, and a particular model request succeeded.

AGENTS.md follows the directory chain

At packages/pager, a repository-root AGENTS.md can supply repository conventions, while files in child directories add package-specific requirements. Core follows the directory chain from project root to cwd. Initialization does not recursively read all descendants. If it finds no root marker, it considers cwd alone. An empty root-marker list also disables parent traversal. .git is the default marker, subject to applicable configuration. The discovery rules define this scope.

Within each directory, only the first existing candidate is selected: AGENTS.override.md, then AGENTS.md, then configured fallback filenames. An override does not concatenate with the ordinary file in the same directory. Selected files from parent and child directories can still contribute in order. A fallback must be a filename; candidates with unsuitable path syntax are skipped according to the execution environment's path conventions. The candidate-selection logic prevents a configurable name from becoming an arbitrary path probe.

project_doc_max_bytes supplies a shared remaining budget consumed in environment and file order. Oversized files are truncated. Text conversion uses lossy UTF-8 decoding, and the result retains its source file and environment identity. An explicitly Untrusted project skips project documents, while host-provided user instructions can remain. This document check is implemented separately from the explicit Trusted requirement for project configuration, so the two trust conditions should not be collapsed into one rule. The document reader and budget show the difference.

The budget creates a content tradeoff. Root documents read first can consume space that would otherwise hold instructions closer to pager. A truncation boundary need not end at a paragraph. Putting every piece of knowledge in the root file changes what the model can actually see. Short constraints and useful discovery pointers make better use of that space. Chapter 13 covers on-demand skill and extension loading.

Cache invalidation follows access boundaries

Loading instructions at startup does not mean loading them only once per process. AgentsMdManager::refresh resolves a consistent snapshot at startup or a request boundary. Host providers own their fetching and caching. Repository-instruction caching uses changes in environment selection and project trust level to decide whether to rediscover files. This also does not imply a full disk rescan for every model request. The refresh conditions define the actual behavior.

Consider a permission reduction. After an environment-selection change, old instructions may originate somewhere the new environment can no longer read. When rediscovery is needed, the manager clears the repository cache first. If discovery fails or is cancelled, stale content must not remain exposed. Keeping the old value on error is often useful for an ordinary performance cache; after an access-boundary change it can violate the new restriction.

# Teaching pseudocode: refreshing instructions
if environment_selection_changed or project_trust_changed:
    remove_old_repository_cache_immediately()
load_host_user_and_thread_instructions()
validate_new_instructions()
if repository_discovery_needed:
    read_with_current_environment_and_permissions()
publish_only_validated_results_as_the_new_snapshot()
return_warnings_to_the_caller()

File-read failures also depend on context. Without a restricted sandbox read context, loading errors can be logged and processing can continue. Errors on the restricted read path propagate upward. These branches have different availability and access semantics. A missing document, exhausted byte budget, and inability to confirm a document under current permissions are distinct outcomes for the repair task.

Read failures as assembly contracts

Suppose a newly cloned repository contains an incomplete .codex/config.toml. Parsing every file and rejecting every error would let an unauthorized source prevent startup. Ignoring every error would conceal a mistake in configuration already trusted to take effect. Codex distinguishes the two: an active source's error needs repair; disabled content should not gain control before activation.

The test invalid_project_config_ignored_when_untrusted_or_unknown checks more than a successful return. It creates both Untrusted and unknown-trust cases, writes broken project TOML, and checks that the project layer remains present with a disabled_reason and empty content. It also verifies that the effective value comes from the user layer. Those assertions connect availability, provenance, and the assembled result. We read this test without executing it.

Obtaining a Config confirms that configuration was assembled successfully. The service connection may still fail, thread storage may be unavailable, or extension startup may be cancelled. At that point, useful feedback identifies the startup phase that could not be established. It should not ask the model to guess a repository failure. The startup guard introduced in Chapter 1 retains cleanup responsibility for resources that have not been fully handed off.

Reading the source

  • arg0/lib.rs: identity dispatch and runtime. Follow why helper paths must outlive the entry-point call.
  • core/config/mod.rs: ConfigBuilder. Trace cwd, layers, and final Config assembly.
  • config_layer_source.rs: source precedence. Compare SessionFlags with legacy managed layers.
  • loader/mod.rs: configuration before project discovery. Follow why root and trust decisions precede project loading.
  • loader/mod.rs: project parsing and filtering. Compare trusted and disabled failure paths.
  • state.rs: effective configuration and origins. Requirements provenance is recorded separately.
  • auth/manager.rs: authentication reads. Distinguish cache access, refresh, and account-bound network configuration.
  • agents_md.rs: document loading. Inspect trust, byte budgets, and read failures.
  • agents_md_manager.rs: snapshot refresh. Check the order of invalidation and publication.
  • agents_md test: overrides and parent-child order. Continue to the directory-chain assertions after line 449 in the same file. These are source-reading pointers, not reported test results.

Design lessons

  1. Retain configuration provenance. When layered settings make changes hard to explain, store field origins, layer versions, and disabled reasons. The diagnostic interface must evolve with the actual resolver.
  2. Separate source trust from source authority. Decide whether a repository source may participate, then filter which keys it may control. This requires maintained filtering rules beyond a trusted boolean.
  3. Resolve cwd before discovery. Directory-dependent configuration and instructions need an absolute scope. Changing that scope requires recalculation and invalidation of affected caches.
  4. Allow startup to rebuild its configuration. Login, destination selection, and trust can change applicable policy. Rebuilding configuration and services requires a complete resource handoff and cleanup path.
  5. Give project instructions a scope and budget. Define directory order, candidate priority, and a total size limit. Since content can be truncated, the most necessary rules should be brief and clear.

Chapter 03 · Runtime foundations

Chapter 3: Sessions, threads, and turns

Chapter outline
  • Thread identity and live runtime
  • Creating and reusing a thread
  • Communication endpoints have their own lifetime
  • Four input-routing intentions
  • Commit settings with acceptance
  • Reserve idle state and retain finishing ownership
  • Interrupting a turn and shutting down a Session
  • Reading events accurately
  • Reading the source
  • Design lessons
  • Interactive panel: What a receipt confirms

Configuration is assembled, but the model has not yet begun repairing the pagination function. Which object will own that work? Two consecutive user messages could describe separate tasks or one task with an added constraint. An interface might disconnect while work continues. A settings change might arrive after a request has already been sent. Each case requires a precise answer about state lifetime.

Codex assigns these responsibilities to a thread, its live Session, a turn, and a model step. They have different completion conditions, storage, and access paths. Following those objects makes it possible to identify which work can be observed, refused, or cancelled.

This chapter follows acceptance and ownership in the empty-input repair scenario. Chapter 4 examines model streaming, and Chapter 5 follows how tool feedback drives further work. Here we establish the lifecycle that contains those actions.

Thread identity and live runtime

Four objects divide the responsibilities:

Object Question it answers Typical contents
ThreadManager How are threads created, found, and managed? Live-thread registry, shared services, startup requests
CodexThread How does a caller operate on a thread? Session, SessionIo, startup metadata
Session What does the live thread own? State, services, active turn, input queue
TurnContext / StepContext What does a turn or model request use? Identity, settings, environment, capabilities, authorization relationships

A conversation thread has a nameable, discoverable identity. It does not require a dedicated operating-system thread. ThreadManager maintains live threads through shared state, while CodexThread wraps an Arc<Session> and communication endpoints. Cloning the handle shares access to the same runtime; it does not copy the history or create another agent. The handle structure exposes that relationship directly.

Inside Session, state and services have separate homes. SessionState contains configuration, the context manager, usage, and session-level records. active_turn has its own lock, and the input queue has a dedicated abstraction. Service objects provide the model client, execution, extensions, and persistence. A source comment limits a Session to at most one running task. Model streams, tools, prewarming, and other background asynchronous work can still run concurrently. The restriction concerns ownership of the session task. The Session fields and comments establish its scope.

Creating and reusing a thread

Ordinary startup calls start_thread(StartThreadOptions) on the manager. Options include Config, initial history, environments, dynamic tools, and extension-initialization data. The entry point also participates in resume and internal-session creation. The manager turns these inputs into a spawn request and assembles the history and services needed by Session. Creation, resume, and fork can therefore share lifecycle machinery while keeping their own input rules.

Warm resume illustrates the distinction. If initial history names a thread already running in memory, the manager can return its existing CodexThread and startup information. It rejects inconsistencies such as a different rollout path and restricts access to special internal reviewers. Cold resume has to rebuild the runtime. Thread identity, live runtime, and disk history are separate enough that resuming need not create a copy of everything. The live-thread reuse branch is a useful entry point; Chapter 11 covers storage.

Startup can still fail before handing over a usable handle. The manager transfers Session and SessionIo together and invokes the startup guard if that process fails. For a caller, a returned NewThread confirms completion of this startup operation. Constructing Session internally does not prove that registration and resource handoff succeeded. Configuration completion in the previous chapter was an earlier milestone.

Communication endpoints have their own lifetime

SessionIo holds the submission sender, event receiver, agent-status watch receiver, and a shared future for the background loop's completion. The source explains why these endpoints are separate from Session: when all submission senders are dropped, the loop can end, and multiple callers can observe the same shutdown through the shared completion future. SessionIo gives communication capabilities a lifetime distinct from runtime state.

Startup creates a bounded submission queue with capacity 512 and an unbounded event queue. A submitter can wait for the receiver to make room. Event production has no equivalent wait for consumer capacity. The pair therefore has different backlog risks, and consumers need to keep reading events. The channel creation and capacity constant define the actual backpressure boundary.

An ordinary submit generates a submission ID, wraps the operation in Submission, and queues it. Alongside Op, that wrapper carries trace information and parent and root turn relationships. Some internal paths also carry a guard that keeps the receiving thread resident. Metadata moves causal information and lifecycle responsibility across asynchronous boundaries. When a new turn starts, App Server exposes the corresponding submission ID as the turn ID; submissions that join existing work need not create turns. Read Submission alongside the ID convention.

Interactive exploration · Teaching model

What a receipt confirms

Follow an evidence timeline for starting, steering, rejection, interruption, or dropping the receipt waiter.

Owning turn
Unconfirmed
Routing receipt
Unconfirmed
Model-step evidence
Unconfirmed
Persistence evidence
Unconfirmed

    Arrows arrange teaching observations by evidence level. Real asynchronous events can interleave; TurnStarted may arrive before the caller reads its receipt. A confirmed write barrier does not establish losslessness of all data under power failure.

    Started and Steered confirm core acceptance and routing without waiting for prompt hooks, context updates, rollout persistence, or sampling. Dropping the waiter for an enqueued operation does not withdraw it. Terminal-event payloads still need inspection; termination does not establish task verification.

    Stages the receipt does not wait forDropping a waiter does not withdraw queued workDifferent completion and abort payloads

    Explore the mechanism in your browser. This panel does not execute Codex. Scenarios and values are illustrative; the chapter and source give the full conditions.

    The background submission_loop receives and dispatches operations while also watching agent-tree shutdown and mailbox notifications. It waits for the routing handler's decision, not for the entire model turn. Otherwise, a model waiting for approval could block the very operation carrying the user's approval reply. A separate task runs the long-lived turn work; the submission loop sends control operations to the appropriate owner.

    Four input-routing intentions

    The common entry point for the repair request is start_or_steer_turn. It starts an ordinary turn when idle or steers an active ordinary turn that can accept input. A later "Keep the function signature" can join the repair without making the interface inspect state and choose between two APIs. Core performs the check and decision together, reducing the race between reading state and submitting work.

    The other methods express narrower intentions. start_turn_if_idle starts only when idle and cannot automatically become a steer. steer_turn requires a particular active turn ID and cannot silently start new work after that target ends. continue_turn_if_idle accepts internal response items and requires that newer work has not replaced the preceding turn. Its content is not treated as new user authorization. The routing methods put these intentions in the interface.

    Results are Started, Steered, or NotSubmitted. Rejections also have types: not idle, no active turn, target-ID mismatch, a task that cannot be steered, output-schema mismatch, or a server no longer accepting new turns. A client can preserve a draft, report that a target changed, or retry later according to the reason. The result and rejection types describe both paths.

    Input type matters as well. Plan mode restricts automatically started work, while actual user input can start a turn. Internal recovery has a separate entry point and authorization semantics. During server draining, new ordinary turns are generally refused, with limited exceptions for some delegated work already inside a parent task. Acceptance depends on both the input and the lifecycle it is trying to enter. Chapter 15 follows the multi-agent branches.

    # Teaching pseudocode: let core interpret the caller's intent
submit_by_mode(input):
    if steer_only: verify_the_target_turn_still_matches()
    if start_only_when_idle: atomically_check_and_reserve_idle_slot()
    if start_or_steer: first_try_the_active_turn()
    check_input_type_output_constraints_and_admission_policy()
    if rejected: return_reason_without_changing_state()
    if accepted: apply_settings_and_start_or_append_work()
    return_owning_turn_identity()

    Started and Steered confirm acceptance for turn processing. They do not wait for prompt hooks, model-context updates, rollout writes, or sampling. Queue submission happens earlier still: SessionIo::submit_turn_input waits on a oneshot for the routing decision. Dropping that wait after enqueueing does not withdraw the submitted work. If the session loop exits before replying, the waiter receives InternalAgentDied. The post-enqueue contract is part of the API's cancellation semantics.

    Continuation and recovery also differ. Continuation starts a new turn from internal response items while idle, checking the expected previous turn so a late background result cannot displace newer work. Recovery resumes an interrupted ordinary turn, preserving its recorded turn ID without manufacturing another user message. Both can run the model again, but they preserve different identity and authorization evidence. The recovery entry point records the distinction.

    Parent and root turn IDs add causal coordinates. They associate messages, metrics, and delegated results with the work that initiated them. They do not automatically grant a child every execution permission of its parent. If the repair delegates a caller search, its result should be traceable back to the original task, while environment, configuration, and budget inheritance still follow the child-creation rules.

    Commit settings with acceptance

    Suppose you steer a repair turn that has already ended and attach a setting to use another model next time. Changing the setting before checking the target would leave an unexpected configuration change after returning failure. PreparedTurnInputSettings first prepares and previews changes. It applies them only when input is accepted. The prepare and apply phases establish a transaction boundary.

    For a new turn, thread settings and startup options contribute to TurnContext. Core validates and commits configuration, then constructs the context without holding the state lock. Admission uses current and validated candidate configuration to make a quick, side-effect-free decision under the lock. This keeps invalid configuration out of live state without holding a large lock during slow resource preparation. The context-construction path separates atomic commitment from assembly.

    Successful steering can commit persistent thread settings, while the active turn retains its existing context. Future turns see that update. An added message does not rewrite the active turn's starting identity. An attached output schema is a compatibility requirement: it must match the schema the active turn already uses. Thread preferences, turn constraints, and input provenance therefore retain separate rules.

    TurnContext contains more than a configuration copy. It holds the turn ID, initial settings, next-model-step settings, starting environment, extension state, timing, and terminal error. StepContext captures settings and capability versions for one request. Changing a future turn's model preference and changing the next model step within the current turn are separately implemented paths. The steer-setting rule does not imply that every setting change must wait for a future turn.

    Reserve idle state and retain finishing ownership

    A caller cannot check for no active turn, release the lock for lengthy preparation, and later start unconditionally. Another input might claim the same idle state. start_if_idle checks active_turn under the lock, checks the expected previous turn when required, and inserts a reserved ActiveTurn. Preparation failure or policy rejection clears that reservation. The idle reservation joins the check to ownership of the next turn.

    Task startup records turn ownership and creates a cancellation token, completion notification, and task handle. When its future returns, on_task_finished takes the task from the active turn, changes its state to finishing, records pending input, and organizes terminal events. ActiveTurn can represent a reservation before task startup or finishing work after the task returns. Consequently, task.is_none() is not a general idle check. The ActiveTurn and RunningTask types show those states.

    This is a teaching state diagram, not a separate enum copied from the source. During finishing, Arc::ptr_eq checks that cleanup still refers to the same turn state, so late-finishing work cannot clear newer state. An ordinary turn generally delivers its terminal event before conditionally clearing the active slot, then continues rollout flushing and pending-work checks. Receiving that event does not prove every background cleanup operation succeeded.

    Interrupting a turn and shutting down a Session

    An interrupt cancels the task token, allows time for cooperative exit, aborts the handle if necessary, and invokes task-specific abort cleanup. The Interrupted branch may also record an interruption marker and attempt a flush before emitting TurnAborted. Flush failure produces a warning. The code arranges a persistence barrier but does not give the event a fault-independent durability guarantee. The cancellation and terminal-event path shows the sequence.

    Waiter cleanup has its own ordering. abort_all_tasks first lets tasks waiting for approvals or other results observe cancellation, then clears pending input and waiters. Dropping a sender first could make a task interpret the missing reply as a denial and produce an unintended model-visible result. When the user stops the pagination repair, the history should not acquire an invented claim that the user refused a patch.

    # Teaching pseudocode: interrupting a turn
remove_current_active_task()
notify_task_of_cancellation()
wait_for_cooperative_exit_or_deadline()
stop_task_handle_and_run_task_cleanup()
record_applicable_interruption_marker()
emit_abort_event_with_turn_identity()
clear_pending_input_and_waiters_for_that_turn()

    Session shutdown has a broader scope. It stops admission, cancels prewarming and active work, terminates background execution processes, closes hooks and MCP services, closes thread persistence, and reports ShutdownComplete. shutdown_and_wait waits for the shared background-loop completion future. Even when every submission sender is dropped without an explicit Shutdown operation, leaving the submission loop still schedules teardown. A turn interrupt leaves the live thread available for further work; shutdown closes that runtime. The shutdown and channel-close branches retain cleanup when an interface omits its final command.

    Reading events accurately

    A core Event contains an ID associating it with a submission and an EventMsg. Consumers can group progress by work, but must still inspect payloads. TurnComplete can carry a terminal error. TurnAborted records the reason, timing, and turn identity. End of work and achievement of the requested goal need separate facts.

    Event reception also has ownership rules. CodexThread::next_event removes the next event from the queue. Multiple readers do not automatically receive broadcast copies. queued_event_count supports handoff of a finite queued batch, with a requirement for exactly one reader while consuming that batch. A state watch supplies the latest state; the event queue preserves facts to process in order. A new interface might observe "idle" while missing earlier errors or tool records if it confuses the two. The consumer contract explains why a cloned endpoint is not a full-history subscription.

    Relevant tests gate fake model responses to submit two user messages concurrently. They expect exactly one Started and one Steered with the same turn ID, then find both inputs in the second model request body. Another test steers after a turn has ended, expects NoActiveTurn, and checks that previous thread settings remain unchanged. These assertions test the relationship between admission and state without requiring a particular model sentence. We have read their implementation, not executed them, and they do not establish coverage of every concurrent schedule.

    The repair now has an explicit owner at every level: a thread identity, a live Session, a turn that can accept steering or be aborted, and a captured context for each model step. The next chapter follows requests across the model boundary.

    Reading the source

    • thread_manager.rs: thread startup. Continue through the spawn request and warm-resume branch.
    • codex_thread.rs: input-routing methods. Compare start-or-steer, idle-start, and internal continuation.
    • session/mod.rs: SessionIo submission and receipts. Identify enqueue and receipt failure points.
    • session/handlers.rs: submission_loop. Follow sequential dispatch alongside background turn work.
    • turn_input.rs: PreparedTurnInputSettings. Trace preview, new-turn commit, and steer commit.
    • turn_input.rs: idle reservation and release. Inspect how a reservation makes the idle check atomic.
    • state/turn.rs: ActiveTurn and waiters. Read task, cancellation, and turn-local state together.
    • tasks/mod.rs: common finishing path. Continue to terminal events and active-state removal.
    • tasks/mod.rs: interruption. Locate cancellation, waiting, abort, recording, and notification.
    • turn_input_submission.rs: settings update after acceptance. Read with the preceding concurrency test to inspect state contracts. These pointers describe assertions, not results from an execution for this book.

    Design lessons

    1. Separate handles from live state. Multiple interfaces can share controlled access to one runtime. Specify what cloned handles mean for shutdown and event consumption.
    2. Route input atomically in core. Explicit start, steer, and idle-start intentions avoid a caller-side read-then-submit race. Clients must handle the resulting typed rejections.
    3. Commit attached changes only after acceptance. Validate candidate settings, then bind their application to admission. This needs a preview or commit phase beyond a simple setter.
    4. Represent reservations and finishing work. Preparation and final writes can outlive the task handle. Retain ownership across those phases and use a stricter idle predicate than task presence.
    5. Define interruption as a protocol. Tasks holding processes or waiting for approval need ordered cancellation, waiter cleanup, and terminal reporting. Session shutdown needs a separate contract, including observable cleanup and persistence failures.
